children.text: pavitrā nāma satyā saṃskṛtā arghyahetuḥ sampannā na tu viparītetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Pure" means truthful, refined, a cause of honor, and complete, not the opposite: this is the meaning.
That is to be concealed.
If one asks, "For what purpose?"
That is answered: for indicating birth, knowledge, tapas, and praise.
Just as the osprey indicates autumn.
For it has been said:

children.text: śaradaṃ kuraraḥ prāha vasantaṃ prāha kokilaḥ
children.translated_text: "The osprey announces autumn; the cuckoo announces spring;

children.text: prāha varṣā mayūraśca vāk pavitrāha brāhmaṇam ||
children.translated_text: and the peacock announces the rainy season, while pure speech announces a brāhmaṇa."
Likewise:
"Speech itself, when spoken, declares a man's learning,
illumining everything, like spotless radiance illumining the sun."
Therefore there are birth, knowledge, tapas, and praises.
And when praised, there is no exhaustion or increase of merit and sin, since they have a beginning and an end.
Therefore this has been said: "one whose pure speech is hidden."

children.text: āha kiṃ vrataṃ vāṇī ca dvayamevātra gopyam āhosvid anyadapyasti neti ||
children.translated_text: One asks: are the vow and speech alone, these two, to be concealed here, or is there also something else?
It is said: there is.
Because he says:
Thus.
Here the word "all," because its subject is the doors, should be understood as denoting without remainder.
The doors are the acts of crying out and the like.
And why are they called doors?
Because <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) are causes of gain and loss, they are doors.
The plural "doors" is used as in the case of knowledge, instrument, and sense faculty.
"Having covered" refers to the application of the earlier means.
How?

children.text: asthānakāladeśakriyāprayogaprayojanāntarāṇi vidhivad vivecya yadā samyaṅ māyayā saṃnādyabhedakrameṇa prayuktāni tadā pihitāni bhavantītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When improper place, time, region, action, application, and other purposes have been distinguished according to rule, and when they have been properly applied through <s>māyā</s> (artifice) in the sequence of sounding and differentiation, then they are covered: that is the meaning.
One asks: by what are they to be covered?
That is now stated.

children.text: yasmādasya śrotrendriyavat pidhāyeti samyag jñānaprayoge sarvajñena bhagavatā vidyānugṛhītayā buddhyā pidhānamuktaṃ tasmādatra karaṇākhyā buddhyeti na jñānākhyā ||
children.translated_text: Since, as in the case of the auditory faculty, in the proper application of knowledge the omniscient Blessed One taught covering by the intellect aided by <s>vidyā</s>, therefore here it is the intellect called the instrument, not that called knowledge.
How is this understood?
From the instrumental construction, "by the intellect."
As with bathing by means of ashes.
It is not that called knowledge.

children.text: yasya vijñānākhyā buddhirna jñānākhyā kathaṃ gamyate ||
children.translated_text: How is it understood that his intellect is called cognition and not called knowledge?

children.text: tasya prāg jñānotpatter acetanapuruṣastasya hy ajñānād asaṃbodhyaḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: Because before the arising of knowledge his person would be unconscious; for, owing to ignorance, he would be incapable of being awakened.

children.text: tasmādatra trikaṃ cintyate pidhātā pidhānaṃ pidheyamiti tatra pidhātā sādhakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore a triad is to be considered here: the coverer, the covering, and what is to be covered. In that triad, the coverer is the practitioner.
His covering is the intellect aided by <s>vidyā</s>.
What is to be covered is the vow, speech, and the doors.

children.text: kramavṛttitvāc ca buddhereva prayuṅkte śeṣāṇy akartṛtvenaivāprayuktāni ||
children.translated_text: And because the intellect acts in sequence, it alone applies them; the rest, being non-agents, are not applied by themselves.
Then they are covered: that is the meaning.
Here this section on <s>vidyā</s> and knowledge is completed.
One asks: is only the twofold state, "unmanifest" and "like a departed spirit," to be adopted here?

children.text: vāgādīni vā gopāyitvā sādhakena kiṃ kartavyam ||
children.translated_text: Or, after guarding speech and the other faculties, what should be done by the practitioner?
It is said:

children.text: atra buddhyā antaḥkaraṇānāṃ śrotrādīnāṃ ca bāhyānāṃ vṛttivibhramaḥ kartavyo'sati viṣaye viṣayagrahaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Here, by the intellect, a disturbance of the functions of the internal organs and of the external faculties such as hearing is to be produced: the apprehension of an object when no object is present.
On this point:
Five madnesses are declared: those whose nature is wind, bile, and phlegm,
the fourth is a combination of the humors, and the fifth is caused by injury.

children.text: evaṃ grahabahutve sati yo 'yaṃ vātapittaśleṣmaṇāṃ samūhaḥ sāṃnipātiko'yaṃ mahāgrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, when there are many seizures, this aggregate of wind, bile, and phlegm is the great seizure called combined.
In this way the application of the means is to be performed.

children.text: tatra yadi kaścid jñānajijñāsanārthaṃ dayārtham anugrahārthaṃ vā pṛcchati taṃ nivartayitvā brūyāt samayataḥ praviśasveti ||
children.translated_text: There, if someone asks for the sake of seeking knowledge, out of compassion, or for the sake of favor, he should turn him back and say, "Enter according to the rule."

children.text: tato dvāreṇa praviśya viparītam aviparītaṃ vā yadi kaścid brūyāt ko bhavāniti tato vaktavyaṃ māheśvaro'haṃ kaumāro 'hamiti duratyayaṃ kṛtaṃ ca mamāneneti ||
children.translated_text: Then, having entered through the door, if someone says, whether correctly or incorrectly, "Who are you?" then he should say, "I am a <s>Māheśvara</s>; I am a <s>Kaumāra</s>. This man has done me an offense that is hard to overcome."

children.text: tato jighāṃsanārthaṃ mayā spṛṣṭo na tu viṣayakrīḍārthaṃ vā ||
children.translated_text: "Therefore he has been touched by me for the purpose of killing him, not for the sake of play with sense-objects."

children.text: tataḥ parivarjayati ityevaṃ laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ sammohanārtham uktam unmattavad iti ||
children.translated_text: Then he avoids him. In this way "like a madman" is taught for the purpose of deluding worldly examiners.
Somewhat like a madman or a departed spirit, only a disturbance of the functions of his inner organ and the like is admitted.
"Alone" is to be understood as "not accompanied."

children.text: ekenetarebhyo vicchinnenāsahāyenety arthaḥ āha ekena kiṃ kartavyamiti ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: by himself, cut off from others, without a companion. One asks: what should he do alone?
It is said: he should wander.
For he says, "he should move about."
Here <s>vi</s> is in the sense of expansion.
The verbal root <s>car</s>, "to move," concerns acquisition, specifically the acquisition of <s>dharma</s> (merit).
The form ending in <s>-īta</s> expresses command and injunction.
The meaning is that, because of the injunction of expansion and in particular, he should wander.
One asks: where should he wander?
It is said: in the world.
The designation "world" applies to those belonging to the three varṇas and life-stages, not to <s>Brahmaloka</s> and the like.
Why?
Because it is impossible among the exalted ones.
"In the world" means a nearby presence.
The worlds are the higher varṇas; among them, under those who preside over them, he should wander: that is the meaning.

children.text: āha kāṃ vṛttimāsthāya loke vihartavyam sarvabhakṣameva ||
children.translated_text: One asks: having adopted what way of life should he wander in the world? Should he eat everything indiscriminately?
It is said: no.
Because he says:
Here, from the mention of what is prepared, there is prohibition of what is unprepared, such as seeds, stalks, fruits, and the like.

children.text: kṛtaṃ bhinnodbhinnādyaṃ tad bhaikṣam utsṛṣṭaṃ yathālabdhaṃ vidhinā prāptamupayojyam ||
children.translated_text: What is prepared, such as what has been split or has sprouted, namely alms-food that has been abandoned, obtained as it comes, and received according to rule, is to be used.

children.text: atra kṛtagrahaṇādakṛtapratiṣedhaḥ akṛtapratiṣedhāc ca kṛtsnā hiṃsā tantre pratiṣiddhā draṣṭavyā ||
children.translated_text: Here, from the mention of what is prepared there is prohibition of the unprepared; and from the prohibition of the unprepared, all injury is to be understood as prohibited in the <s>tantra</s>.

children.text: āha kiṃ tat kṛtaṃ nāma buddhighaṭādyam ||
children.translated_text: One asks: what is this thing called prepared? Is it something made by the intellect, a pot, and so on?
That is answered: no.
For he says: food.
There, from the word "food" there is prohibition of what is not food.

children.text: tac ca dviyoni indrābhiṣiktam indriyābhiṣiktaṃ ca tatrendrābhiṣiktaṃ vrīhiyavādyam ||
children.translated_text: And that has two sources: what is consecrated by <s>Indra</s> and what is consecrated by the senses. There, what is consecrated by <s>Indra</s> is rice, barley, and the like.
But what is consecrated by the senses is meat.

children.text: tat pañcavidham bhakṣyaṃ bhojyaṃ lehyaṃ peyaṃ coṣyamiti ||
children.translated_text: That is fivefold: what is chewed, what is eaten, what is licked, what is drunk, and what is sucked.
Likewise it has six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent.
One asks: from where should the acquisition of that prepared food be made?
That is said: abandoned.
Here, from the mention of abandoned food, there is prohibition of alms-food and of what is merely obtained as it comes.
For what reason?
Because its purpose is the avoidance of faults such as the slaughterhouse, not because of faults such as theft and accepting gifts.
And that abandoned food is threefold.
That is, namely: released, dismissed, and wholly abandoned.

children.text: tatra sanimittaṃ parityaktamannaṃ pānaṃ vā tan nisṛṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: There, food or drink abandoned for a specific reason is "released."
What is abandoned on account of a cow, a Brahmin, and the like is "dismissed."
What is abandoned from another source is "wholly abandoned."

children.text: dayārtham ānṛśaṃsārthaṃ vā yadi kaścid dadyāt tadapi grāhyameva ||
children.translated_text: If someone gives something for the sake of compassion or for the sake of non-cruelty, that too is indeed to be accepted.
One asks: what is to be done by this practitioner with it?
It is said: it should be used.
For he says, "he should take up"; here the prefix "upa" has the sense of acceptance and admission.
The meaning is: by one who is established in the discipline of extreme <s>asanmāna</s> (non-honor).

children.text: ādadīta ityupayoge grahaṇe ca vivakṣitasūtragrahaṇe tvāvad bhavati ||
children.translated_text: "He should take" is intended both in the sense of use and in the sense of receiving; with regard to the intended sūtra, however, it is at least an act of taking.
That has been stated:
Having gathered up this very man, who is never satisfied with desires,
death seizes him and carries him away, as a tiger seizes an animal.
Thus.
Even in the sense of use, as in the expression "Nātha-Kaṇāda-Vatsa."
Therefore it is to be used.
The form "īta" is used in the sense of command and injunction.
That which has been given up and is obtained by rule should be used.

children.text: anyathā hi vidhivyapetena krameṇa vṛttyarjanaṃ na kartavyamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Otherwise, the meaning is that livelihood should not be procured by a sequence devoid of rule.

children.text: āha vratādīni gopayitvā samyaksādhanaprayoge utsṛṣṭopayoge ca vartataḥ ke vārthā niṣpadyante ||
children.translated_text: One asks: when one conceals the vows and the rest, and proceeds with the proper application of the practice and with the use of what has been given up, what purposes are accomplished?
Or is there a conclusion to the section on <s>asanmāna</s> (non-honor), or not?
It is said: there is.
For he says:
Here, "mad" refers to that very same person.
Its previous explanation was stated above: "deluded."
The root "muh" has the sense of failing to understand.

children.text: avyakto'yaṃ preto'yam unmatto'yaṃ mūḍho'yaṃ mūrkho'yamiti vaktāro vadantītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that speakers say, "This one is obscure; this one is like a corpse; this one is mad; this one is deluded; this one is foolish."
The word "iti," because it gives the explanation of the meanings, serves to conclude the topic.
Thus, since abiding, time, place, action, application, purpose, concealment, residence, and all the austerities that bring about the aim have been explained,
"Thus" looks back to what has already passed.
"He thinks" has the sense of ascertainment.
"The others" includes householders, students, forest-dwellers, mendicants, and heterodox ascetics who are authorized in celibacy.
"People," likewise.
The root "jan" means coming into being.

children.text: janā iti varṇāśramiṇāṃ janānām adhikṛtānāṃ grahaṇam uktaṃ hi
children.translated_text: "People" is said to include the authorized people who belong to the classes and life-stages. For it has been said:

children.text: janena hi jano jātaḥ janaṃ janayase jana
children.translated_text: "By a person a person is born; O person, you generate a person.

children.text: janaṃ śocasi nātmānaṃ mātmānaṃ śoca mā janam ||
children.translated_text: You grieve for a person, not for yourself; do not grieve for yourself or for a person."
The meaning is that speakers say this in such a way.
Here this authoritative section on the practice of <s>asanmāna</s> (non-honor) is completed.

children.text: āha vratādīni gopayitvā samyaksādhanaprayoge utsṛṣṭopayoge ca tataḥ ko guṇaḥ yaṃ guṇaṃ jñātvā avyaktapretonmattādyā vādā niṣpādyā iti ||
children.translated_text: One asks: after one has concealed the vows and the rest, and then used the proper application of the practice and what has been given up, what virtue results, knowing which statements such as "obscure," "corpse-like," and "mad" are to be produced?
That is answered: having known that virtue, we shall state it.

children.text: api ca avyaktapretonmattādyaṃ brāhmaṇakarmaviruddhaṃ kramaṃ dṛṣṭvā yāvadayaṃ śiṣyaḥ enamarthaṃ na bravīti tattasya hṛdistham aśaṅkitam upalabhyottaraṃ brūma iti kṛtvā bhagavānidaṃ sūtramuvāca ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, seeing a course that is contrary to brahmanical conduct, until this student states this meaning, and having perceived that it is present in his heart without being suspected, <s>Bhagavān</s> spoke this sūtra with the thought, "We shall give the answer."
Here the letter "a" negates honor or pride.
Here honor or pride is twofold.
There is pride of birth and pride of being a householder.
Of these, pride of birth is the thought, "I am a Brahmin."

children.text: pūjyatvād ūrdhvagamanādīnāṃ kāryāṇām ucchritatvāt trayāṇāmapi varṇānāmupadeśena gurutvād yajñakartṛtvāt trailokyasthitihetoḥ brāhmaṇo'hamiti prathamo māno jātyutkarṣāt ||
children.translated_text: Because he is worshipful, because acts such as upward progress are lofty, because he is elevated, because he has the status of teacher for all three classes through instruction, because he is the performer of sacrifice, and because he is the cause of the maintenance of the three worlds, the first pride is "I am a Brahmin," arising from superiority of birth.
So too there is the pride produced by the fact that Brahmins, including householders and the rest, are worshipful.
And this twofold pride is prohibited by the statement about the obscure mark.

children.text: tathā vittaṃ bandhuryaśaḥ karma vidyā bhavati pañcamī
children.translated_text: "Wealth, kin, fame, action, and knowledge as the fifth:
these are the bases of honor, each later one weightier than the last."

children.text: etāni caikavāsaḥpretācaraṇagūḍhavratopadeśinā sūtrataḥ pratiṣiddhānītyato māno na kartavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And these too are prohibited by the sūtra that teaches one garment, corpse-like conduct, and hidden vows; therefore pride should not be produced.
"Being" is used in the sense of praise and also of existence.
What precedes is also qualified by that section on the practice of <s>asanmāna</s> (non-honor).
This word "hi" should be understood as referring to supreme excellence.

children.text: yantrāṇi agniṣṭomādīni māsopavāsādīni ca gṛhasthādīnāṃ śuddhivṛddhikarāṇi ||
children.translated_text: The disciplines, such as the <s>agniṣṭoma</s> and the monthly fasts, increase purity for householders and the rest.
And why are they called "disciplines"?
"Discipline" means rites and the like.

children.text: yasmād ayantrā laukikā amaryādāvasthā bhavantītyato yantrāṇām ||
children.translated_text: Because, without discipline, worldly states become unbounded and outside proper limits; therefore the word is "of disciplines."
"Of disciplines" is the genitive plural.

children.text: āha bahuvacanaprayogāt saṃdehaḥ atha kiyatāṃ yantrāṇām ||
children.translated_text: One asks: because the plural is used, there is doubt; of how many disciplines is this so?
That is answered: of all.
Here "of all" means "without exception."
"Of all" is the genitive plural.
One asks: because the genitive requires completion, there is doubt.
For those disciplines, what exists as the causal essence?
That is answered: the highest.
Here "highest" denotes superiority in supreme purity, abandonment, non-appropriation, and the like.
For it has been said:
"Choice, best, chief, most excellent, or beautiful;
highest and lattermost, each in its own sense, express the meaning 'best.'"
It means "best."
And here it is stated as "highest."

children.text: āha asanmānaḥ sarvayantrāṇāmuttama iti kva siddham ||
children.translated_text: One asks: where is it established that <s>asanmāna</s> (non-honor) is the highest of all disciplines?
It is said: here.
For he says, "it is remembered."

children.text: atra smṛta ityuktaparyāyaḥ maheśvareṇoktaṃ proktaṃ kathitaṃ varṇitamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here "remembered" is equivalent to "stated": it means that it was said, declared, told, and described by <s>Maheśvara</s>.
Why is it distinguished?
Because it is the word of the omniscient one and because it is not contradicted.
The meaning is that the words of those who see directly are not false.

children.text: āha asmin krame uttamatvena vyākhyāyamānaṃ ka ādyaḥ śodhakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He asks: in this sequence, as it is being explained as the highest, who is the first purifier?
Or by whom was this injunction practiced?
And, by practicing it, what result was obtained?
He should be stated for the sake of producing conviction in us.
That is now said.
Here <s>Indra</s> is the king of the deities.
How is this understood? Because practice among the asuras is mentioned.
And this <s>Indra</s> is a Brahmin and is the best.
Because the Brahmin is mentioned in the <s>sūtra</s>, and because there is a prohibition regarding the śūdra.
The verbal root id is in the sense of supreme lordship; from that comes <s>Indra</s>.

children.text: indra utkṛṣṭaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ devagandharvayakṣarākṣasapitṛpiśācādīnāṃ śreṣṭho na tu brahmādīnām ||
children.translated_text: <s>Indra</s> means exalted, the best: he is the best among gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, piśācas, and the like, but not among <s>Brahmā</s> and the others.

children.text: kiṃ tu svargiṇāṃ madhye aiśvaryeṇa vidyayā ājñayā cety ataḥ śreṣṭhatvād indraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Rather, among those in heaven he is best through lordship, knowledge, and command; therefore, because of his superiority, he is <s>Indra</s>.
The word vā expresses possibility.
This injunction was also practiced by other excellent gods.
How much more, then, by you and the rest, who are merely human?
Therefore this meaning is to be considered possible.
He asks: when was it practiced?
It is said: at the beginning.
Here 'beginning' refers to an earlier time.
Before the connection with <s>Kuśika</s> and <s>Īśāna</s>.
First it was practiced by the immortals.
The meaning is: in the ages beginning with Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara.
He asks: among whom was it practiced?
It is said: among the asuras.
Here the asuras are so called as beings other than the suras, connected with theft.
Or they should be known as asuras, sons of <s>Prajāpati</s>, because they take away the vital breath.
The phrase 'among the asuras' indicates a nearby presence.
The meaning is: near the asuras, in the vicinity of the asuras, as overseer of the asuras.
He asks: what was that?
It is said: the <s>Pāśupata</s>.
Here, because it operates within the rules and observances taught by <s>Paśupati</s>, it is <s>Pāśupata</s>.
Or, because <s>Paśupati</s> is contemplated in it, it is <s>Pāśupata</s>.
Or, because it brings one to <s>Paśupati</s>, it is <s>Pāśupata</s>.
The word <s>Pāśupata</s> here denotes this entire complete injunction.
Why?
Because the sequence beginning with the unmanifest is preceded by a manifest liṅga (mark).
Therefore this entire injunction was practiced by <s>Indra</s>, who desired the end of suffering, for the sake of the increase of purification.
Because of the abundance of <s>dharma</s> among the gods, it was practiced on earth.
'He practiced' denotes past time.
The meaning is: he practiced it in a past time.
He asks: what result was obtained by <s>Indra</s> as he practiced among the asuras?
That is now said.
'He' is the reference to <s>Indra</s>; 'of them' is the indication of the asuras.
Iṣṭāpūrta is a dvandva compound.

children.text: iṣṭaṃ ca pūrtaṃ ceṣṭāpūrtam tatra yan mantrapūrvakeṇa vidhinā dattaṃ hutaṃ stutyādiniṣpannaṃ sukṛtaṃ tad iṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: The iṣṭa and the pūrta together are iṣṭāpūrta. There, whatever meritorious act is given, offered, or accomplished through praise and the like by a rite preceded by mantras is iṣṭa.
Whatever is not preceded by mantras is pūrta.
By what means was it given by <s>Indra</s> to the asuras?
It is said:

children.text: krāthanaspandanādiprayogaiḥ dhikkṛtasya nidrāviṣṭo vāyusaṃspṛṣṭo mandakārī asamyakkārī asamyagvādīti yo 'yaṃ duṣṭaśabdo 'bhiyogaśabdaśca niṣpadyate tasminn anṛte māyāsaṃjñā ||
children.translated_text: Through practices such as krāthana and spandana, when the censured person is called 'possessed by sleep, touched by wind, slow in action, acting wrongly, speaking wrongly,' the bad word and the accusatory word that arise in that falsehood have the designation māyā (deceptive appearance).
And also in mental and bodily accusation.
'By māyā' is in the instrumental case.
As for 'by the well-made one':

children.text: su praśaṃsāyām tayā sukṛtayā samyak prayuktayeti sādhakasādhanaprādhānyam ||
children.translated_text: su is used in the sense of praise; by that well-made one, that is, by one properly employed, the primacy of practitioner and means is indicated.
'He obtained' has the sense of attainment and also of predominance.
Thus, he took their iṣṭāpūrta.
For it has been said:
Being reviled, he does not revile in return; he patiently endures anger alone.

children.text: sa teṣāṃ duṣkṛtaṃ dattvā sukṛtaṃ cāsya vindati ||
children.translated_text: Giving them his demerit, he obtains their merit.
He asks: <s>Indra</s> is the highest.

children.text: sa teṣāmiṣṭāpūrtam ityukte parāpadeśenāsya vṛttir nirguṇīkṛtā ||
children.translated_text: When it is said, 'He took their iṣṭāpūrta,' his conduct has been left without explicit qualification by being referred to through others.
Now, is there here any reference to himself, or not?
It is said: there is.
For he says:
Here nindā (blame) is censure such as insult, humiliation, and the like.
The meaning is contempt and reproach.
The word should be understood with reference to blame, to the exaltation of the highest, and to rejection.
This is understood from the section on the highest.
The word 'this' looks back to what has already been passed over.
The meaning is blame such as insult, humiliation, slander, and the like.
In 'non-blame,' the negative a negates being blameworthy.
The meaning is non-censure, non-contempt, and non-reproach.
Here the word 'therefore' looks to both what precedes and what follows.
In relation to what is expected from what precedes, first, it states the virtue of the entire topic of blame.

children.text: yasmād indrasyāpi śuddhivṛddhikāriṇī ātmāpadeśena parāpadeśena ca bhagavatā asanmānacarir guṇīkṛtā tasmādityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because even for <s>Indra</s>, conduct under dishonor, which increases purification, was made a virtue by <s>Bhagavat</s> through reference to himself and through reference to others; that is the meaning of 'therefore.'

children.text: āha nirākāṅkṣānirdeśāt saṃdeho yathā yathā varṇitaṃ tathā tathā ca vyākhyātam ||
children.translated_text: He asks: because the statement is made without further expectation, there is doubt; it has been explained in just the way in which it was described.

children.text: nindāyā aninditatvaṃ guṇaṃ jñātvā sādhakena kiṃ kartavyam ||
children.translated_text: Having known the virtue that blame is not blameworthy, what should the practitioner do?
That is now said.
Here blame is the one previously mentioned.
With 'being blamed,' the present time of blame is meant for the very person who is being blamed.
'He should practice' refers to acquisition.
It is used with reference to the acquisition of <s>dharma</s> and to injunction.
And because the doubt is different, the word 'practice' should be understood as not redundant.
Here this ancillary topic concerning conduct under dishonor is completed.

children.text: āha nindyamānaś caredityuktvā ādyaṃ vidhānamācarataḥ ko 'rtho niṣpadyate ||
children.translated_text: He asks: after saying 'one should practice while being blamed,' what purpose is produced for one who practices the first injunction?
Or, when it has been produced, how is it to be described?
That is now said.

children.text: atra caryottarasambandhād gamyate yadetadaninditaṃ karma dharmaḥ sa eva nindyamānasyācarato niṣpadyate ||
children.translated_text: Here, from the connection with the later practice, it is understood that this faultless act, which is <s>dharma</s> (religious merit), is accomplished precisely for one who practices while being censured.
Therefore the meaning is: he is one whose act is faultless.

children.text: āha nindyamānasyācarato 'ninditaṃ karma bhavatīti kva siddham ||
children.translated_text: One asks: where is it established that a faultless act belongs to one who practices while being censured?
That is answered: here, because he says so.
Here, "this" is used in a directly perceptible sense.
For example, "this person."

children.text: yathāvidhiś caririti yāḥ kriyāḥ atrādhikṛtasyāninditaṃ karma bhavatītyāha bhagavān ||
children.translated_text: The Blessed One says that the actions here for the qualified person, called conduct according to rule, are a faultless act.
Why?
Because they have the capacity to bring one near to <s>Rudra</s>.
And, because they have the capacity to bring about non-return, it is complete.
Therefore, because the words of the omniscient one do not fail, the meaning is that this is the true path.

children.text: āha kimanyatra panthāno na santi iti ||
children.translated_text: One asks: are there no other paths elsewhere?
It is said: there are.
But still:
Here the syllable "ku" has the sense of censure.
Why?
It is understood from the use of the word "ku."
As in the expression "a bad man."
"Paths" means rules and means.
The word "tu" marks the superiority of non-return.
"Others" means:
the paths of householders, brahmacārins, forest-dwellers, mendicants, and heretics.
They are bad paths.
No.

children.text: āha ayameva satpathaḥ śeṣāḥ kupathā iti kva siddham ||
children.translated_text: One asks: where is it established that this alone is the true path and the remaining ones are bad paths?
Or what is its being a true path?
And why are the remaining ones bad paths?
It is answered here.
Because he says:
Here, "by this" has the sense of not depending on anything else.
"By the rule" means by the means consisting of the ash-bath, krāthana, and so on.
In "by the rule" there is the instrumental case.
"<s>Rudra</s>" is an instruction concerning the time or condition.
The <s>Rudra</s>-nature of <s>Rudra</s> has been stated earlier.
"Nearness" is a synonym of yoga.
How is this understood?
Because it is stated immediately after the rule.

children.text: sati vidhiviṣayatve puruṣeśvarayor viṣayādhikārakṛtaṃ viyogaṃ dṛṣṭvā jñānaparidṛṣṭena vidhinādhyayanadhyānādhikṛto viśuddhabhāvaḥ samīpastha ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When the rule has a person as its object, and when one has seen the separation between the person and the Lord caused by object and qualification, the one qualified for study and meditation, by means of the rule seen through knowledge, has a purified disposition and stands nearby: this is the meaning.
"Going" means attainment, namely the attainment of the state.
"-tvā" indicates completion with respect to the rule and the act.

children.text: āha atraivaṃ vidhyācaraṇaṃ samīpagamanaṃ ca kasyopadiśyate ||
children.translated_text: One asks: for whom are practice of the rule in this way and approach to nearness taught here?
It is answered: not for everyone, as in the case of <s>dharma</s> such as pilgrimage to sacred places.
Rather, as in the case of initiation, it is only for a brāhmaṇa.
Because he says:
Here the teaching of the negative particle is for the sake of prohibiting the acceptance of another practice.
"Any" means a householder and the others.
Because a mere difference of station is seen, the word "any" applies only among brāhmaṇas.

children.text: gṛhastho brahmacārī vānaprastho bhikṣur ekavedo dvivedas trivedaś caturvedo gāyatrīmātrasāro vānena vidhinā rudrasamīpaṃ prāptaḥ san na kaścid brāhmaṇaḥ punarāvartata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: no brāhmaṇa at all, whether a householder, a brahmacārin, a forest-dweller, a mendicant, one who knows one Veda, two Vedas, three Vedas, four Vedas, or one whose essence is merely the Gāyatrī, returns again after attaining nearness to <s>Rudra</s> by this rule.

children.text: brāhmaṇagrahaṇaṃ brāhmaṇyāvadhāraṇārthaṃ brāhmaṇa eva nānya ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The mention of brāhmaṇa is for the ascertainment of brāhmaṇa-hood: a brāhmaṇa only, and no one else.
And the designation brāhmaṇa applies to the knower of the field.
Why?
He is a brāhmaṇa because of connection with growth and birth, connection with initiation, and connection with the Veda.
The word "again" is used to prohibit return again.

children.text: yathā pūrvasaṃjñānādibhir gatvā āvartate punaḥ punaḥ tathānena vidhinā rudrasamīpaṃ gatvā na sakṛdāvartate ||
children.translated_text: Just as one goes by means of earlier designations and the like and returns again and again, so, having gone near to <s>Rudra</s> by this rule, one does not return even once.
The meaning is that he does not return again and again in any way at all.

children.text: āṅ iti svaśāstroktamaryādām adhikurute abhividhyarthaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: "Ā" lays claim to the boundary taught in one's own scripture and also has the sense of complete extension.

children.text: ye cānena vidhinākṣapitājñānakaluṣapāpamāyādayaḥ kṣīṇāḥ te punaḥ punarāvartante ||
children.translated_text: And those things such as ignorance, impurity, sin, and māyā, which have been destroyed by this rule, are exhausted; they do not return again and again.
There is no connection with them.
Nor does he take on another birth: this is the meaning.
Having thus brought the chapter to completion, it is proper to speak.
The meaning stated earlier belongs to this.
One asks: what, then, is that brahman?

children.text: tad ucyate kāraṇādibhāvenoktasya bhagavata ekatvaṃ sādhako jñātvā tatsādhanam ārabhate ||
children.translated_text: That is answered: having known the unity of the Blessed One, who has been described as cause and so on, the practitioner begins the means to that.

children.text: atra pūrvaṃ kāraṇatvabahutvanānātvenopadiṣṭasya parāmarśaḥ tad iti ||
children.translated_text: Here "that" is a reference back to what was previously taught as cause, multiplicity, and diversity.
"Person" means person because of filling out with personhood.
His personhood consists in his abiding in many forms.
The forms based on that are Aghora and the others.
In "to <s>Tatpuruṣa</s>" there is the dative case.

children.text: yathā grāmāya tattvaṃ jñātumicchati tathā puruṣāya tattvaṃ jñātumicchati ||
children.translated_text: Just as one wishes to know the reality for a village, so one wishes to know the reality for the <s>Puruṣa</s>.
"Let us know":
the root vid means knowing.
"Vidmahe" means "we know" or "we apprehend."
One asks: because there is a plurality of persons, there is doubt.
Then, for which person?
That is answered:

children.text: atra mahādevatvaṃ ca pūrvoktam mahādevāyeti caturthī ||
children.translated_text: Here greatness as a god has also been stated earlier; in "to <s>Mahādeva</s>" there is the dative case.
"Let us meditate":
the root dhīṅ has the sense of union.
"Dhīmahi" means "may we meditate," "may we dissolve," or "may we be joined with the powers of knowledge and action."
Here "dhī" is a synonym for the power of knowledge.
That by which one apprehends the reality of all things is the power of knowledge.
"Mahi" is a synonym for the power of action.
That by which one becomes capable of practicing the rule and yoga is the power of action.

children.text: āha athaite dṛkkriyāśaktī mahādevāt sādhakaḥ kiṃ svaśaktita āsādayati āhosvit paraśaktitaḥ utobhayaśaktitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One asks: now, does the practitioner obtain these powers of seeing and action from <s>Mahādeva</s> through his own power, or through another power, or through the power of both?
That is answered: through another power.
Because he says:
The word "that" is the apprehension of the powers of seeing and acting.
The word "na" is used in the indication of the self.
The meaning is "of us."
The word "<s>Rudra</s>" is used in the indication of the cause.
The <s>Rudra</s>-ness of <s>Rudra</s> has been stated above.
The word "pra" and the following are used with reference to action.
The root cud means "to impel."
Prompting is the conjunction of the powers of knowledge and action.
The word "yād" means the desire to obtain.
The meaning is: "Join me."

children.text: uktaṃ hi rudrasyecchāpūrvako yo yogo jñānakriyāśaktibhyāṃ paśvādiṣu sambhavaḥ taccodanam āhur ācāryāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For it has been said: the union of <s>Rudra</s>, preceded by desire, which is possible in <s>paśu</s>s and the like through the powers of knowledge and action, the teachers call that prompting.
Here the syllable a is used to deny attachment.

children.text: atra saṅgo nāma yadetat puruṣe viṣayitvam ||
children.translated_text: Here attachment means this object-directedness in the person.

children.text: tena viṣayitvena yogādadharmeṇa cāyaṃ puruṣo yadā adhyayanadhyānādibhyaścyavati ||
children.translated_text: When, through union with that object-directedness and with adharma, this person falls away from study, meditation, and the like,
the meaning is the three times, as with a forest elephant, characterized by hearing and seeing an example.
Non-attachment, too, is the non-contemplation of past, future, and present objects, like a mendicant.
Thus the abiding of one's disposition in <s>Maheśvara</s> is his non-attachment: this is the meaning.

children.text: āha kim asaṅgitvam evaikamuktaṃ nānyal lakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: One asks: is only non-attachment stated, and no other characteristic?
It is answered: because he says:
Thus.
Here yoga should be understood as the yoga that is the conjunction of the self and the Lord.
For it has been said:
With the blasts of conches and kettledrums, with various movements and musical performances,
he should not become aware while they are being performed; this is the mark of one who is yoked.
Thus.
One asks: are only two characteristics of the yoked one stated here?
No.
Because he says:
Here, by the qualification of eternity, non-eternity is excluded.

children.text: nityatvaṃ nāma sati vibhutve puruṣeśvarayor manasā saha gatasyātmatābhāvasya vṛttyākārasya viṣayaṃ prati kramo 'kṣopo 'vasthānaṃ vṛkṣaśakunivat ||
children.translated_text: Eternity means that, when the person and the Lord are all-pervasive, the state of selfhood, accompanied by the mind and having the form of a mental modification, proceeds toward its object in sequence, without disturbance, and remains fixed, like a bird in a tree.

children.text: tasmin nirvṛtte maheśvare yukto nitya ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: When that is accomplished in <s>Maheśvara</s>, the yoked one is called eternal.
The word "self" indicates the knower of the field.
How is this understood?

children.text: cittasthityupadeśād yogārthaṃ vidyācaraṇopadeśād asaṅgayogiyuktātmājamaitrādīnāṃ cetane sambhavāt na tv acetaneṣu kāryakaraṇapradhānādiṣu ||
children.translated_text: Because steadiness of mind is taught, because knowledge and conduct are taught for the sake of yoga, and because being non-attached, a yogin, yoked, a self, unborn, friendly, and so on are possible in a conscious being, but not in unconscious things such as effect, instrument, and primary matter.
In that conscious being the word "self" is used.
And why is it the self?
Because it pervades, it is the self.
Because, having filled the effect and the instrument, it makes the objects conscious, it is the self.
For it has been said:

children.text: yad āpnoti yad ādatte yac cātti viṣayān punaḥ
children.translated_text: Because it obtains, because it takes, and because again it consumes objects,

children.text: yac cāsya satataṃ bhāvaḥ tasmādātmeti saṃjñitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and because this is its constant condition, therefore it is named the self.

children.text: sa ca śrotā spraṣṭā draṣṭā rasayitā ghrātā mantā vaktā boddhā ityevamādiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And it is the hearer, toucher, seer, taster, smeller, thinker, speaker, knower, and so on.
For it has been said:

children.text: puruṣaś cetano bhoktā kṣetrajñaḥ pudgalo janaḥ
children.translated_text: The person is conscious, the enjoyer, the knower of the field, the individual, the human being,

children.text: aṇur vedo 'mṛtaḥ sākṣī jīvātmā paribhūḥ paraḥ ||
children.translated_text: the minute one, the knower, the immortal, the witness, the living self, the surpassing and the supreme.
Thus.
The meaning is that it is apprehended by signs such as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and consciousness.
One asks: are only these three characteristics of this yoked one stated?
No, because he says:
Here "unborn" expresses the denial of manifestation as some other object.
Here "other object" means what is other than sound, touch, form, taste, and smell: study, meditation, recollection, and the like.
Because he is not born among these, he is unborn.
One asks: are only these four characteristics of this yoked one stated?
No.
Because he says:
Here "friendly" applies in the sense of evenness.
For example, the sun is friendly.

children.text: sarvabhūtasthite ca maheśvare sthitacittaḥ icchādveṣavinivṛtto 'pravṛttimān maitra ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: One whose mind is fixed on <s>Maheśvara</s>, who abides in all beings, who is free from desire and aversion and without outward activity, is called friendly.

children.text: tasmāt kāryakaraṇavān eva cittasthitisamakālam evāsaṅgādibhāvena jāyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, only one who possesses effect and instrument is born in the state beginning with non-attachment, precisely at the same time as steadiness of mind.
One asks: then how, again, is this understood?

children.text: yathā kāryakaraṇavān eva cittasthitisamakālam evāsaṅgādibhāvena jāyate ||
children.translated_text: That is, how is it understood that only one who possesses effect and instrument is born in the state beginning with non-attachment, precisely at the same time as steadiness of mind?
It is answered: it is understood.
Because he says:
Here the prefix abhi is used as a qualifier.
If one asks, what is the distinction?
That is answered:

children.text: yasmādayaṃ saṅgī ayogī anityātmā anajo 'maitraś ca bhūtvā asaṅgādibhāvena jāyata ityeṣa viśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since this person, having been attached, non-yogic, non-eternal in self, not unborn, and unfriendly, is born in the state beginning with non-attachment, this is the distinction.
"Is born" means:
the root jan means manifestation.

children.text: tasmāt kāryakaraṇavān eva cittasthitisamakālam evāsaṅgādibhāvena yugapaj jāyate avaśyādivad ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore only one who possesses effect and instrument is necessarily born all at once, precisely at the same time as steadiness of mind, in the state beginning with non-attachment: this is the meaning.
What is that means in the state beginning with non-attachment, by which he is born?
It is answered:
Here conqueredness is conquest.
Therefore, from that conquest, non-attachment and the rest arise.

children.text: atra parigrahatayeśvarāṇi indriyāṇi buddhyādīni vāgantāni trayodaśa karaṇāni ||
children.translated_text: Here, as the things to be taken possession of, there are the lordly senses, or the thirteen instruments beginning with intellect and ending with speech.
The meaning is: from the complete conquest of them.
One asks: how is the establishment of intellect understood?
That is answered: because it is established.

children.text: atra matibuddhipidhānasthāpanoddeśād ghaṭapaṭavat siddhatvāc ca buddhiḥ siddhā tathā paropadeśāt svātmaparātmaprativibhāgadarśanāt suro'haṃ naro'hamiti bhinnavṛttitvāc cāhaṃkāraḥ siddhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, because thought, intellect, covering, placement, and indication are mentioned, and because it is established like a pot or a cloth, intellect is established. Likewise, from another's instruction, from the perception of the distinction between one's own self and another's self, and from the difference of functions such as "I am a god" and "I am a man," egoity is established.

children.text: tathā manaḥ pravartate manojavī mano'mana iti saṃkalpavikalpavṛttinānātvaṃ ca siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise the mind operates; and the diversity of functions of determination and doubt is established by expressions such as "swift as mind," "mind," and "non-mind."
Thus the internal organ, whose functions extend through the three times, has been explained for the person.
Similarly, among the cognitive senses, hearing has been explained.

children.text: paraparivādādivacanād uccairubhayathā pramukhe dvir adhiṣṭhāne saṃniviṣṭaṃ sāmantācchabdavyañjanasamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: From the statement concerning speech such as censure of others, the ear is established as situated high up, on both sides, in front, in two seats, and as capable of manifesting sound all around.

children.text: tathātitapopadeśāt tvag antarbahiśca śarīraṃ vyāpya saṃniviṣṭā sparśavyañjanasamarthā siddhā ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the instruction about intense heat, the skin is established as situated pervading the body inside and outside, and as capable of manifesting touch.

children.text: tathā mūtrapurīṣadarśanapratiṣedhāt kṛtānnādivacanāc ca cakṣuḥ uccair ubhayathā pramukhe dvir adhiṣṭhāne saṃniviṣṭaṃ ghaṭarūpādi vyañjanasamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the prohibition against looking at urine and feces, and from the statement about prepared food and the like, the eye is established as situated high up, on both sides, in front, in two seats, and as capable of manifesting such things as the form of a pot.

children.text: tathā māṃsalavaṇopadeśāj jihvā tanmukhe māṃsapeśyāṃ saṃniviṣṭā rasajñānajananasamarthā siddhā ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the instruction about meat and salt, the tongue is established as situated in the piece of flesh in that mouth and as capable of producing knowledge of taste.

children.text: tathā prāṇāyāmopadeśād ghrāṇaṃ pramukhe uccairubhayathā dvir adhiṣṭhāne saṃniviṣṭaṃ gandhagrahaṇasamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the instruction about breath-control, the nose is established as situated in front, high up, on both sides, in two seats, and as capable of apprehending smell.
Thus, because the <s>puruṣa</s> understands through these by the activities proper to the authorized agent, they are the cognitive faculties.
Likewise there are the action faculties.

children.text: maṇṭanaviharaṇopadeśāt pādendriyam adhastād dvir adhiṣṭhāne saṃniviṣṭaṃ gamanakriyāsamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: From the instruction about moving about, the faculty of the feet is established as situated below, in two seats, and as capable of the action of going.

children.text: tathā mūtrapurīṣadarśanapratiṣedhāt pāyvindriyaṃ guhyapradeśe saṃniviṣṭam utsargakriyāsamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the prohibition against looking at urine and feces, the faculty of the anus is established as situated in the private region and as capable of the action of evacuation.

children.text: tathā strīpratiṣedhād upasthendriyaṃ trivalīguhyapradeśasaṃniviṣṭam ānandakriyāsamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the prohibition concerning women, the generative faculty is established as situated in the threefold fold and private region, and as capable of the action of pleasure.

children.text: tathā api tatkarmopadeśāt hastendriyam uccairubhayathā dvir adhiṣṭhāne bhujāntardeśe saṃniviṣṭam ādānakriyāsamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the instruction about its action, the faculty of the hands is established as situated high up, on both sides, in two seats, in the region within the arms, and as capable of the action of taking.

children.text: tathā api tadbhāṣaṇopadeśād vāgindriyaṃ vāktālujihvādiṣu sthāneṣu saṃniviṣṭaṃ vacanakriyāsamarthaṃ siddham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, from the instruction about its speaking, the faculty of speech is established as situated in places such as speech, palate, and tongue, and as capable of the action of utterance.

children.text: atra vikāratadvṛttibhiḥ karmotpattiḥ puruṣe iti karmendriyāṇi evametāni trayodaśa karaṇānīndriyāṇi sūtrato vyākhyātāni ||
children.translated_text: Here action arises in the <s>puruṣa</s> through their modifications and activities; therefore they are action faculties. In this way these thirteen instruments, the faculties, have been explained according to the sūtra.
Why?
Because there is a general mention, "of the faculties," and because, as with the instruments, there is no general prohibition.
"Of the faculties" is the genitive plural.
For it has been said:

children.text: ādānād grahaṇāt tyāgād raṅgaṇād gamanāt tathā
children.translated_text: "Because of taking, grasping, abandoning, playing, and going,
and also because of gesturing and running, therefore it is called an <s>indriya</s>."
"Because of conquest," it says.
The prefix "abhi" has the sense of complete victory and subjugation.
They are to be overcome and brought under control.
As with wind, desire, anger, and <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>.

children.text: tasmād akuśalebhyo vyāvartayitvā kāmataḥ kuśalaṃ yojitāni tadā jitāni bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when they have been turned away from unskillful objects and applied at will to skillful ones, then they have been conquered.

children.text: tasmād uktam indriyāṇām abhijayāditi asaṅgādijanmanimittatvāt pañcamī draṣṭavyā ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the statement "because of the conquest of the faculties" is made. Since this is the cause for the arising of non-attachment and the rest, the fifth case should be understood.

children.text: āha anyatra sāṃkhyayogādīnām asaṅgādiyuktāḥ muktāḥ śāntiṃ prāptāḥ ||
children.translated_text: One asks: elsewhere, according to <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, <s>Yoga</s>, and the others, those endowed with non-attachment and the like are liberated and have attained peace.

children.text: nirabhilapyā muktā ityucyante mukta eva na yukta iti kva siddham ||
children.translated_text: They are called inexpressibly liberated. But where is it established that one is liberated only, and not yoked?
That is explained here, since he says:
There, the word "<s>Rudra</s>" is an indication of the Cause.
The state of being <s>Rudra</s> has been stated earlier.
"Pra" is used in the sense of purity of expression.
As in the case of clear faculties.
The root "vac" is used in the sense of articulate speech.
Thus, "he proclaimed."

children.text: evaṃ yat sāṃkhyaṃ yogaśca varṇayati asaṅgādiyuktāḥ muktāḥ śāntiṃ prāptā iti tadaviśuddhaṃ teṣāṃ darśanam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, what <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and <s>Yoga</s> describe, namely that those endowed with non-attachment and the like are liberated and have attained peace, is an impure doctrine of theirs.
It is like the sight of the moon by the eye of a person with cataracts.

children.text: ayaṃ tu yukta eva na mukta iti viśuddhametaddarśanaṃ draṣṭavyam ||
children.translated_text: But this view, that he is indeed yoked and not liberated, should be regarded as pure.
Why?
This is understood from the word of the omniscient one and because it is not contradicted.
The meaning is: this is so, and not otherwise.

children.text: kiṃcānyad idam athaśabdādi śivāntaṃ pravacanaṃ rudraproktaṃ tāvat sarvatantrāṇāṃ śreṣṭham ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, this teaching, beginning with the word "atha" and ending with "śiva," was spoken by <s>Rudra</s> and is foremost among all tantras.
Therefore, the superior authority of the Cause and the scripture is to be ascertained; that is the meaning.
Here there is an etymological verse.

children.text: āha kim etānīndriyāṇi parijñānamātrād eva jitāni bhavanti pradhānavat ||
children.translated_text: One asks: do these faculties become conquered merely by being fully understood, as in the case of primary matter?

children.text: taducyate na jñānena vacanādibhireṣāṃ jayaḥ kartavyaḥ yasmādeṣāṃ jaye bhagavatā vasatyarthavṛttibalakriyālābhāya vasatā ityatas tajjaye vasatyartha eva tāvad ucyate ||
children.translated_text: That is answered: no. Their conquest is to be accomplished by recitation and the like, not by knowledge alone. Since, for the conquest of these, <s>Bhagavān</s> teaches dwelling in order to obtain the force and action of the practice of dwelling, therefore, with regard to their conquest, the purpose of dwelling is first stated.
For he says:
Thus.
Here, a dwelling that is empty is an empty house.
"Empty" means secluded and without people.

children.text: āgāram iti gṛhaparyāyaḥ āgāraṃ gṛhaṃ veśma sadanamiti paryāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "House" is a synonym for dwelling: house, dwelling, residence, and abode are synonyms.
The root "guhū" means covering.
Because it covers and protects the practitioner who has entered, it is a cave.

children.text: āha āvarakatvāviśeṣāc chūnyāgāraguhayor aviśeṣa iti cet taducyate mṛttṛṇakāṣṭhādikṛtam agāraṃ parvataguhādyā guhā ||
children.translated_text: One asks: if, because there is no difference in being a covering place, there is no distinction between an empty house and a cave, that is answered: a house is made of clay, grass, wood, and the like, while a cave is a mountain cave and so on.
Therefore there is no lack of distinction.

children.text: yathā sati vibhutve jñatvaṃ sādharmyaṃ puruṣeśvarayoḥ sarvajñatvato viśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as, although there is pervasiveness, knowingness is a common property of the <s>puruṣa</s> and the Lord, yet there is a distinction because of omniscience.

children.text: tasmād āyatane 'viviktadoṣaṃ dṛṣṭvā śūnyāgāre guhāyāṃ vā yathopapattito vicārya viviktaṃ vivecya yanmātrasthānāsanaśayanādibhir upajīvati tanmātraṃ saṃskaraṇamaryādayopayogakriyābhiniviṣṭena vastavyam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, seeing the defect of non-seclusion in a residence, he should examine, according to what is available, an empty house or a cave, choose a secluded place, and dwell there, using only so much as he lives on in the way of place, seat, bed, and the like, while being intent on the act of use within the bounds of proper preparation.
Because of association with residence, he becomes one who dwells in a cave.
Like one who dwells on a river-bank.

children.text: āha tat kathaṃ jñeyaṃ yathā jitānīndriyāṇi ||
children.translated_text: One asks: how is it to be known that the senses have been conquered?
Or what is the mark of them when they have been conquered?
That is stated.
Here the god is the Blessed Lord.

children.text: tatra yadāsya bhagavati deve nityatā katham ||
children.translated_text: There, when there is constancy toward the Blessed Lord, how is this so?
For one who is directed toward the Lord by study and meditation, steadiness exists in a primary way.
Even with a very slight interruption, there is uninterrupted attainment through the excessive practice of yoga.
Recollection, then, is what is meant by constancy toward the Lord.
One asks: what is the mark of constancy toward the Lord?
That is stated: having conquered the senses.
Because he says:
Here having conquered the senses means being fit for release and restraint.

children.text: indriyāṇi buddhyādīni vāgantāni trayodaśa karaṇāni pūrvoktāni ||
children.translated_text: The senses are the thirteen instruments previously mentioned, beginning with intellect and ending with speech.

children.text: tāni yadā akuśalebhyo vyāvartayitvā kāmataḥ kuśale yojitāni hataviṣadarvīkaravad avasthitāni bhavanti tadā devanityo jitendriya ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When those senses, having been turned back from unwholesome things and intentionally joined to wholesome things, remain like snakes whose poison has been destroyed, then one is constant toward the Lord and has conquered the senses: this is the meaning.
One asks: is constancy toward the Lord itself this person's supreme, final yoga?
It is said: no.
Because he says:
Or else there is another, remote connection.
Because it has been said:
For whatever has a connection with some object, by that connection it is so, even when remote;
for things that are different in meaning, there is no connection, even when they are adjacent.
So here too there is a remote connection. Why?

children.text: iha purastāduktaṃ vijñānāni cāsya pravartante iti etair guṇair yukta iti ca ||
children.translated_text: Earlier in this passage it was said, "his cognitions proceed," and also, "endowed with these qualities."
In how much time do those qualities arise for him?

children.text: kiṃ yuktasya kiṃ viyuktasya kiṃ yugapat kramaśo vā kiṃ sakalasya niṣkalasya veti ||
children.translated_text: Do they arise when he is yoked or not yoked, simultaneously or successively, when he is possessed of parts or without parts?
This discussion is begun in order to explain these matters that have not been explained.
Because he says, "after six months, for one constantly yoked."

children.text: atra ṣaḍ iti saṃkhyā māsān iti kālanirdeśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here "six" is a number, and "months" is an indication of time.
By human reckoning a month has thirty days.
Twelve months are a year.
Twelve fortnights are half a year.
Thus, "after six months."
Therefore, within the interval between the first and sixth months.
"For one constantly yoked."
This means continuously and without interruption.
"Yoked" means:
yoga is the union of the self with the Lord.
"Of one constantly yoked" is in the genitive case.
One asks: what happens to this yoked one?
That is stated.

children.text: atra bhūyiṣṭham iti krame prāye ca bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Here "for the most part" applies both to sequence and to prevalence.

children.text: yathā kramaśo dadāti ādityo vā gato bhūyiṣṭham ||
children.translated_text: As in the expressions, "he gives in order," or "the sun has for the most part gone down."

children.text: tasmāt sūcyagreṇotpalapattraśatabhedanakramavat kramād dūradarśanādayaḥ pravartanta ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the qualities beginning with distant sight arise successively, as in the sequence of piercing a hundred lotus leaves with the point of a needle: this is the meaning.
The prefix sam is used in the sense of unification.
"Without parts" means devoid of effect and instrument.
The prefix pra occurs in the sense of an initial action, a beginning.
The meaning is that, after being yoked, the qualities arise through power.
Where does it arise?
Sight arises with respect to the visible; hearing and the rest with respect to the audible and so on: this is the meaning.

children.text: tasmāt ṣaṣṭhaprathamamāsayorabhyantare nityayuktasya kramaśo guṇāḥ sampravartante ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, within the interval between the first and sixth months, the qualities arise successively for one constantly yoked.
From what?
From the grace of <s>Maheśvara</s>.
When what is called non-Śiva-ness has ceased, the qualities arise through Śiva-ness and grace.
The word "quality" denotes distant sight and the like.

children.text: āha kāṃ vṛttimāsthāya śūnyāgāre guhāyāṃ vāsaḥ kāryaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One asks: adopting what mode of life should one dwell in an empty house or in a cave?
That is stated.
A collection of alms is bhaikṣya, like the word kāpota.

children.text: tac ca nagaragrāmādibhyo gṛhād gṛhaṃ paryaṭato bhakṣyabhojyādīnām anyatamaṃ yat prāpyate kṛtānnādivacanād bhaikṣyam ||
children.translated_text: And that is bhaikṣya: whichever one of edible or chewable foods and the like is obtained while wandering from house to house from a city, village, and so forth, because cooked food and the like are mentioned.
It is bhaikṣya because it destroys fear.
Because alms are mentioned, what is not alms is prohibited.

children.text: āha ādhārāttu kṛtvā saṃdehaḥ atha kutra tad bhaikṣyaṃ grāhyam ||
children.translated_text: One asks: but since it depends on a support, there is a doubt: where should that alms-food be received?
That is stated: in a bowl.
Because he says:
Here the bowl is well known, just like alms-food.

children.text: alābudāruvastrādīnām anyatamaṃ yat prāpyate tat khalu hiṃsāsteyādirahitena krameṇāhāre yatparyāptaṃ grāhyam ||
children.translated_text: Whichever one among gourd, wood, cloth, and the like is obtained, that should indeed be taken for food in a manner free from injury, theft, and the like, sufficient for the meal.
That which has come into that fruitless bowl is called "bowl-received": this is the meaning.
One asks: in the rule for the brahmacārin it says, "excepting honey, meat, and salt."
Does that mean honey, meat, and the others are absolutely impure?
That is answered: no.
Because he says:
There meat is well known, just like alms-food.

children.text: yasya māhiṣavārāhādīnām anyatamaṃ yat prāpyate tat khalu hiṃsāsteyarahitatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Whichever one among buffalo, boar, and the like is obtained, that indeed is acceptable because it is free from injury and theft.
Or with salt.

children.text: atra lavaṇaṃ nāma saindhavasauvarcalādyaṃ māṃsavat prasiddham ||
children.translated_text: Here salt means rock salt, sauvarcala salt, and so on, well known like meat.

children.text: tad etan māṃsasamasaṃsṛṣṭaṃ vā bhaikṣyavidhinā prāptam ||
children.translated_text: That, whether mixed or not mixed with meat, is obtained according to the rule of alms.
It is not impure, not blameworthy, not censured: this is the meaning.
"Or" is used for option.

children.text: māṃsena vā lavaṇena vā ubhābhyāmapi sākṣādvā aduṣyam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that with meat, or with salt, or even with both, whether directly or otherwise, it is not impure.

children.text: āha bhaikṣyālābhakāle aparyāptikāle vā kimanena kartavyam ||
children.translated_text: One asks: when alms-food is unavailable, or when there is not enough, what should he do?
That is stated: he should remain after drinking water.
Because he says:
Here āṇ means "waters," that is, water.

children.text: āṅ iti atra saṃvṛtaparipūtādimaryādām adhikurute kṛtānnotsṛṣṭavad apadāntaritatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Here āṅ indicates the limit beginning with what is covered and purified, because another word intervenes, as in the case of abandoned cooked food.
A nominative should be understood in the place of an accusative.
Here "waters" are those well known in ordinary usage.
The meaning is water as distinguished from grass and the like.
"Or" is used in the sense of division.
That is, alms are one thing and water another.
The word "even" expresses possibility.

children.text: apy apaḥ pītvā stheyaṃ na tu śāstravyapetena krameṇa vṛttyarjanaṃ kartavyamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: one should remain even after drinking water, but one should not acquire a livelihood by a procedure outside the teaching.
The word "as" has the sense of similarity.

children.text: yathā bhaikṣyopadeśaṃ kṛtvā yogakarmaṇyudyamaḥ kartavya iti vyākhyātaṃ tathā apaḥ pītveti ||
children.translated_text: Just as it has been explained that, after giving instruction about alms, one should make effort in the work of <s>yoga</s>, so too with "after drinking water."
Here the time is twofold: the time of non-acquisition and the time of insufficiency.

children.text: tatra yadā grāmaṃ nagaraṃ vā kṛtsnamaṭitvā na kiṃcidāsādayati saḥ alābhakālaḥ aparyāptikālo nāma yadā bhikṣāṃ bhikṣādvayaṃ vā āsādayati tadā apaḥ pītvāpi stheyam ||
children.translated_text: Of these, when, after roaming through an entire village or town, he obtains nothing, that is the time of non-acquisition. The time of insufficiency is when he obtains one alms or two alms; then he should remain even after drinking water.
One asks: what should be done by one who remains in this way?
That is answered: it should be used.
Because he says, "He should eat in due sequence."
"He should eat" concerns the limit of lightness in food, without obstructing the practice of <s>yoga</s>.
The root aś means eating.
He should eat in due sequence.
The prefix anu is used with an action following after.
"In due sequence" expresses regard for what has gone before and also a manner.

children.text: yathāpūrvaṃ grāmādi praviśya bhaikṣyārjanaṃ kṛtvālābhakāle aparyāptikāle vā tadanu paścād apaḥ pītvā stheyamiti kṛtvā bhagavatā etaduktam aśnīyādanupūrvaśa iti ||
children.translated_text: Having first entered a village and so forth as before and obtained alms, then, in a time of non-acquisition or a time of insufficiency, he should remain afterward after drinking water; with this in view the Blessed One said, "He should eat in due sequence."
Here there is an explanatory verse.

children.text: āha śūnyāgāraguhāvasthasyendriyajayena vartato'sya balaṃ kiṃ cintyate kimakaluṣatvameva ||
children.translated_text: One asks: for this person dwelling in an empty house or a cave and living with the conquest of the senses, what strength is intended? Is it simply stainlessness?
That is answered: no.
Because he says:

children.text: atra gaur lokādiprasiddho mṛgavat khurakakudaviṣāṇasāsnādimān iti ||
children.translated_text: Here "cow" is the animal well known in ordinary usage, like a beast, possessing hooves, hump, horns, dewlap, and so forth.

children.text: tathā mṛgo'pi godravyaval lokādiprasiddhaḥ kṛṣṇamṛgādīnām anyatamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise a deer too is well known in ordinary usage as a substance of the same class as a cow, one or another such as a black antelope.

children.text: tayostu sati dharmabahutve samāno dharmo gṛhyate ādhyātmikādidvaṃdvasahiṣṇutvam ||
children.translated_text: Although the two have many qualities, the common quality is taken: endurance of the internal and other pairs of opposites.
We shall explain that later.
The mention of the qualities of cow and deer is for the sake of mutual qualification.
The word "or" has the sense of an option.

children.text: kriyāsāmānyadṛṣṭyā raudrībahurūpīvad ekadharmeṇa caikadharmeṇa vā stheyamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that, from the standpoint of general action, one should remain with one quality or with another quality, as in the case of the <s>Raudrī</s> and <s>Bahurūpī</s>.
One asks: by what strength is his accomplishment of the task achieved?
That is answered:

children.text: atra adbhiḥ āṅ iva adbhireva āpo jalamityādiprasiddhāḥ pūrvoktāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here "with waters" means, as if with āṅ, precisely with waters; waters are what are well known as water, liquid, and so on, as stated before.
"With waters" is in the instrumental case.
The particle āṅ concerns a limit consisting merely of what is already established.
And it also applies to the limit of endurance of opposites like a cow and a deer.
"Like" is used in a comparison.

children.text: yathā adbhiśca mṛdbhiśca prakṣālitāni vastrādīni śuddhāni bhavanti tadvat ||
children.translated_text: Just as clothes and the like, when washed with water and earth, become clean, so too.
By the strength consisting in having the qualities of cow and deer, he becomes pure.
It is said: no.

children.text: yasmādāha gomṛgayor akuśaladharmapratiṣedhaṃ kuśaladharme ca niyogaṃ siddhaśaktipraśaṃsayā asiddhaśaktipratiṣedhaṃ ca vakṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because he says: we shall explain, by praising perfected power, the prohibition of unskillful qualities and the enjoining of skillful qualities in the cow and the deer, and also the prohibition of unperfected power.
He states that:
But one who is not perfected, while acting in every way, is stained: this is the meaning.

children.text: ato yogī siddha ityevaṃ prāpte sukhamukhoccāraṇārtham uktaṃ siddhayogī iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when it follows that the yogin is perfected, the expression "perfected yogin" was stated for the sake of easy oral utterance.
Here:
<s>Yoga</s> is the conjunction of the self and the Lord.
Through that, this person is a yogin.
"Perfected" means one who has attained lordly powers such as vision.
Indeed he is skilled in mastery, possession, protection, and the like.
"Is not stained" means that he is not joined.
One asks: by what is he not stained?
That is answered: by <s>karma</s>.
Here the word "by karma" is stated.
Why?
Because it is made.
"By karma" is in the instrumental case.

children.text: iṣṭasthānaśarīrendriyaviṣayasambandhakṛtena karmaṇā na lipyate na saṃyujyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that he is not stained, not joined, by <s>karma</s> produced by connection with a desired place, body, senses, and objects.

children.text: āha aninditena śubhena karmaṇā na saṃyujyata ityucyate āho atha kimaśubhena karmaṇā lipyate neti ||
children.translated_text: One asks: is it being said that he is not joined by blameless, good <s>karma</s>, or is he perhaps stained by bad <s>karma</s>? No.
That is answered: no.
Because he says, "by sin."

children.text: atra pāpākhyena pātakena vāniṣṭasthānaśarīrendriyaviṣayagato 'śubhaṃ bhuṅkte tenāpyaśubhena karmaṇā na lipyate na yujyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, through what is called evil, or through sin, one experiences what is inauspicious, connected with an undesired place, body, senses, and objects; yet even by that bad <s>karma</s> he is not stained, not joined: this is the meaning.
"Or" is used in a threefold alternative.

children.text: pātakena vā apātakena vā samastābhyāṃ vā vaśīkaraṇāveśanapālanādiṣu pravartamāno na lipyate na saṃyujyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that, whether he proceeds in mastery, possession, protection, and the like with sin, or without sin, or with both together, he is not stained, not joined.
Why?
Because of the power of perfection.

children.text: asiddhaścāyaṃ yogī brāhmaṇo gomṛgadharmāvastho yadi sarvathāpi gomṛgavat pravartate tato lipyate ||
children.translated_text: But if this unperfected yogin, a brahmin standing in the qualities of cow and deer, acts in every way like a cow and a deer, then he is stained.
Therefore the unskillful quality of the cow and the deer is not to be adopted.
And the skillful quality, namely endurance of one's own internal and other pairs of opposites, is accepted.
By that he becomes pure.
One asks: what is his impurity?
That is answered: by pairs of opposites that cause distraction from <s>yoga</s>, arising from causes such as desire, anger, and headache, by cold and the like, or by other things.
He is not stained, not joined: this is the meaning.
Why?
Because he has attained strength: this is the meaning.
Here there is an explanatory verse.

children.text: āha śūnyāgāraguhāvasthasyendriyajaye vartataḥ kāḥ kriyāḥ kartavyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: One asks: for one who stays in an empty house or cave and is engaged in conquering the senses, what rites are to be performed?
Are they bathing, laughing, and the like, or crying out, trembling, adorning oneself, and the like?
This is answered: no.
Because he says:
Here the reading "ṛcam ṛcām" is also not faulty.
Here the verse called <s>Ṛcā</s> is <s>Aghorā</s>.
How is that understood?
From its being included among the ṛks.
Like <s>Sadyojāta</s>, <s>Tatpuruṣa</s>, and <s>Īśāna</s>, it belongs to the formulas of flame and brilliance.

children.text: iṣṭā ceyaṃ tatra tatra japtavyatvena guṇīkṛtatvāt ||
children.translated_text: And this one is accepted because in various places it is treated as subordinate by being prescribed for recitation.

children.text: pūrvottarasūtreṣu japtavyatvena gāyatryā sahādhyānād āśubhāvasamādhyāsādanāc ca iṣṭā ||
children.translated_text: In the preceding and following sūtras it is accepted because it is mentioned together with the <s>Gāyatrī</s> as something to be recited, and because it brings about a state of purity and concentration.
"Study" is a synonym for recitation.
The form īta is used in the sense of command and injunction.
The meaning is that one should study it mentally alone.
One asks: is only the ṛc to be studied by itself?
It is answered: no.
Because he says, "the <s>Gāyatrī</s>."
The <s>Gāyatrī</s> is the one called <s>Tatpuruṣā</s>.
Its etymological explanation has been stated earlier.
The meaning is that one should study it mentally alone.
One asks: in what condition should one study?
This is answered: restrained by oneself.
Self-restraint is a synonym for <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal).
The word "self" means the knower of the field.
Its selfhood is consciousness.
What is to be attained, the effect, the instrument, and the objects are also involved.
The expression "self-restraint" is appropriate when this triad is present.

children.text: yantraṇaṃ nāma yathāyam ātmabhāvo brahmaṇy akṣarapadapaṅktyāṃ yukto vartate tadātmā yantrito bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Restraint means this: when this state of self is joined to <s>Brahman</s> in the row of syllables and words, then the self is restrained.
How so?
Because of the example of a mind absorbed in dancing. Why?
Because the self and the state of self are not separated.
So too there is simultaneity between a quality and the possessor of the quality.
How so?

children.text: yaṣṭuṃ pravṛtto yantrayituṃ ca pravṛtta eva bhavati ||
children.translated_text: One who has begun to worship has also begun precisely to restrain.
Like a mendicant.
Therefore this restraint itself is <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal).
One asks: here, because there are many <s>Gāyatrī</s> formulas, there is doubt.
How is it known whether the ṛc is <s>Aghora</s> or <s>Tatpuruṣa</s>?
It is answered: it is known.
Because he says:
Here <s>Raudrī</s> means the <s>Tatpuruṣā</s>.
Its etymological explanation has been stated earlier.
The word vā should be understood as distributing <s>Raudrī</s> and <s>Bahurūpī</s> separately.
<s>Bahurūpī</s> means <s>Aghorā</s>.
The word vā means optional choice.
Because the result is the same.
Therefore, by the word vā, either the one or the other is meant.
The meaning is: being restrained by himself, he should study.
One asks: for one who is restrained by himself and studies, what accomplishment of the task is there?
This is answered:
Here the word ataḥ is used to indicate a cause.
The meaning is: he should study while restrained by himself.
Thus it means: for this cause, reason, or occasion.
"Yoga" means:
<s>Yoga</s> should be understood as the conjunction of the self with the Lord.
The prefix pra indicates the beginning of an action.
The meaning of "proceeds" has been stated earlier.
Here there is an explanatory verse.

children.text: āha ṛcam adhīyatā brahmaṇyakṣarapadapaṅktyāṃ kiṃ yuktenaiva stheyam ||
children.translated_text: One asks: when studying the ṛc, should one remain joined only to <s>Brahman</s> in the row of syllables and words?

children.text: āhosvid dṛṣṭā asyānyā sūkṣmatarā upāsanā kriyādhyānanamaḥstavyam ||
children.translated_text: Or has another, subtler practice for it been seen, consisting of ritual action, meditation, obeisance, and praise?
It is answered: it has been seen.
Because he says:
Here "Oṃ" is a synonym for recitation, as in the case of <s>Vāmadeva</s> and the others.
The word kāra should be understood as having the sense of restriction.
For what reason?
For it has been said:
For one constantly yoked to the <s>Praṇava</s> and to the seven utterances,

children.text: tripadāyāṃ ca gāyatryāṃ na mṛtyurvindate param ||
children.translated_text: and to the three-footed <s>Gāyatrī</s>, death does not find the supreme end.

children.text: ityata oṃkāra evāvadhāryate dhyeyatvena na tu gāyatryādayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the <s>Oṃkāra</s> alone is restricted as the object of meditation, not the <s>Gāyatrī</s> and the others.
The prefix abhi has the sense of repetition.
One should have a mind brought close to the <s>Oṃkāra</s>.
The root dhyai means thinking.
Meditation means thinking: this is the sense.
For it has been said:
Meditation, marked by thought, is from the root dhyai, and <s>Brahman</s> is marked by the <s>Oṃkāra</s>.

children.text: dhīyate līyate vāpi tasmād dhyānamiti smṛtam ||
children.translated_text: Because it is held or because one is dissolved in it, therefore it is remembered as meditation.
For half a muhūrta, or for a muhūrta, or even in the interval of breath-control,
a person who thinks on the object to be meditated upon destroys sin.
The form īta is used in the sense of command and injunction.
The meaning is: the <s>Oṃkāra</s> alone is to be meditated upon, and no other.
One asks: the <s>Oṃkāra</s> is to be meditated upon.
But what is the place of meditation?
In what place should fixation be performed?
And what should be done by one who is meditating?
This is answered:
There the word "in the heart" is a synonym for the self.
Why?
Because of the force of what precedes and follows.

children.text: yo 'rtho yatra milati sa tatra sthāpayitavyaḥ sa evārtho dhārayitavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning that fits in a given place should be established there; that very meaning should be held fixed.
Moreover, on the authority of the Veda, it has been said:
From limb after limb you arise; from the heart you are born.

children.text: ātmā vai putranāmāsi sa jīva śaradaḥ śatam ||
children.translated_text: You are indeed the self under the name of son; live for a hundred autumns.

children.text: anyatrāpi ātmā vijāyate putra ātmā vai ātmanaḥ pitā
children.translated_text: Elsewhere too: the self is born as the son; the self indeed is the father of the self.

children.text: ātmaprajo bhaviṣyāmi paramaṃ hṛdayaṃ hi saḥ ||
children.translated_text: I shall have offspring as myself, for he is the highest heart.
Therefore the heart has been said to be the self.
The intellect produces a state, a determinative cognition.
The heart knows what is dear and not dear; the condition of the instruments is threefold.

children.text: tathā loke'pi santi vaktāro hṛdayaṃ te jñāsyati ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, even in ordinary speech there are speakers who say, "Your heart will know."
What has been said?
"Your self will know."
Therefore it is understood that "in the heart" is a synonym for the self.
"In the heart" denotes intimate proximity.

children.text: atra tu oṃkāro dhāryo nātmā kiṃtu ya evātmanyātmabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But here the <s>Oṃkāra</s> is to be held, not the self; rather, it is precisely the state of self that is in the self.

children.text: tasyoṃkārāt pracyutasya viṣayebhyo vṛttivikāramātreṇa gatasya pratyānayanaṃ pratyāhāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: The bringing back of that state of self, when it has fallen away from the <s>Oṃkāra</s> and gone toward objects merely through a modification of its activity, is <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal).
After withdrawing, concentration is to be performed in the heart.
And what is to be held is contemplation of the <s>oṃkāra</s>.
Remaining there itself for a very long time is study.
The supreme meditation is what is beneficial to that concentration.
As for the yoga of settled completion, we shall explain it under 'having established.'
'One should do,' thus.
The verbal root ḍukṛñ has the sense of doing.
When it has a seventh-ending form, it becomes 'kurvīta.'
Concentration is to be performed in the heart.
The form īta is used in command and injunction.
The injunction is for the purpose of prohibiting the requirement that concentration be done in places such as the feet, knees, waist, nose, and so on.
The meaning is: it is to be held in the heart, not elsewhere.

children.text: āha oṃkāraḥ kiṃ parapa viṣṇurumā kumāraśca catasro 'rdhamātrā vā ||
children.translated_text: One asks: Is the <s>oṃkāra</s> the supreme, or <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Umā</s>, and <s>Kumāra</s>, or the four half-mātrās?
Or is it a person of the same kind?
It is said: no.
Because he says:
Here 'ṛṣi' is a name of the Blessed Lord.
Why is he an ṛṣi?
The word ṛṣi is used with reference to action.
What is called ṛṣi-hood is so called because action is proclaimed; therefore he is an ṛṣi.

children.text: tathā kṛtsnaṃ kāryaṃ vidyādyamīśata ityataḥ ṛṣiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, because he rules the whole effect, beginning with knowledge, he is an ṛṣi.
Likewise, 'vipra' too is a name of the Blessed Lord.
Why is he a vipra?
The root vid means knowing.
What is called vipra-hood is the power of knowledge.

children.text: vyāptamanena bhagavatā jñānaśaktyā kṛtsnaṃ jñeyamityato vipra iti ||
children.translated_text: Because the whole knowable realm is pervaded by this Blessed Lord through the power of knowledge, therefore he is called vipra.
Likewise, 'great' is used in the sense of superiority.

children.text: yadetad dṛkkriyālakṣaṇamasti anāgantukam akṛtakamaiśvaryaṃ tadguṇasadbhāvaḥ satattvaṃ tattvadharmaḥ tadakṛtakaṃ puruṣacaitanyavat tan nānyasyetyato 'bhyadhikaḥ utkṛṣṭo'tiriktaśceti mahān ||
children.translated_text: That innate, unmade lordship marked by seeing and acting exists; the existence of that quality is its real nature and an essential property. Since it is unmade, like the consciousness of the person, and belongs to no one else, he is superior, excellent, and surpassing; therefore he is 'great.'
'This' indicates direct perception.

children.text: eṣa yo mayā pūrvam oṃ iti śrotrapratyakṣīkṛto 'rthaḥ asau viṣṇūmākumārādīnām anyatamo na bhavati ||
children.translated_text: This object, which I previously made directly present to hearing as 'oṃ,' is not one or another of <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Umā</s>, <s>Kumāra</s>, and the others.
Why?
Because it has ṛṣi-hood, vipra-hood, and greatness: this is the meaning.
